**OPENING — DEFENDER**

The question is whether Christ had a biological father. The answer the text carries is **yes — Joseph, the named Davidic father: a man was involved, and the seed is honored through the named line.** I affirm the WHO, as the record does; I do not narrate the HOW, because the text does not narrate it. Every claim below is tagged and quoted.

---

**I. THE SEED IS FLESH-SEED, DAVID'S OWN — [L1] + [L2] + [L3]**

[L1] "And Jacob begat **Joseph** the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ" (Matthew 1:16).

[L1] "The LORD telleth thee that he will make thee an house. And when thy days be fulfilled... I will set up thy seed after thee, **which shall proceed out of thy bowels**, and I will establish his kingdom" (2 Samuel 7:11-12).

[L1] "Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, **which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh**" (Romans 1:3).

[L1] "Therefore being a prophet... he, **speaking of the resurrection of Christ**... spake thus, That **of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh**, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne" (Acts 2:30-31).

[L1] "For it is **evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda**" (Hebrews 7:14).

[L2] The words are anatomical and flesh-marked: sperma (G4690, "seed") paired with **kata sarka ("according to the flesh")** at Romans 1:3; osphys (G3751, "loins") at Acts 2:30 is the same loins-word used of Levi in Hebrews 7:5, 10 ("Levi... out of the loins of Abraham"). [L3] "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne" (Psalm 132:11).

A seed that proceeds out of bowels and loins, **according to the flesh**, evident to sight (Hebrews 7:14), is the seed of a man. [L4, on the two footings above: the phrase "according to the flesh" would be empty if no flesh-line of a father stood behind it; the record's own words place the origin in David's body.]

---

**II. THE FATHER IS NAMED, IN FOUR REGISTERS — [L1] + [L3]**

[L1] Mary's own mouth: "thy **father** and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48).

[L1] The narrator: "And **Joseph and his mother** marvelled at those things which were spoken of him" (Luke 2:33); "his parents went to Jerusalem" (2:41).

[L1] The town: "Is not this the carpenter's son? is not his mother called Mary?" (Matthew 13:55); "Is not this Jesus, **the son of Joseph**, whose **father and mother we know**?" (John 6:42).

[L1] The angel: "Joseph, **thou son of David**, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife" (Matthew 1:20) — and Joseph names the child: "**thou shalt call his name JESUS**" (1:21), done at 1:25. [L3] "Jesus of Nazareth, **the son of Joseph**" (John 1:45); "Is not this **Joseph's son**?" (Luke 4:22); Joseph "was of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4), and the throne is "the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32).

Four independent registers — the mother, the narrator, the town, the angel — name one man as father. That is not a title; it is the WHO. [L4, on these footings: a man named "father" by the mother herself, and called "son of Joseph" by those who know both parents, is the biological father the question asks about.]

---

**III. THE SPIRIT-ROWS SPEAK COVENANT ORIGIN AND EMPOWERING PRESENCE, NOT BEGETTING — [L1] + [L2] + [L3]**

[L1] "that which is conceived in her is **of (ek) the Holy Ghost**" (Matthew 1:20); "The Holy Ghost **shall come upon** thee, and the power of the Highest **shall overshadow** thee" (Luke 1:35).

[L2] ek (G1537, "of") with God or Spirit is the covenant-origin idiom throughout: "born of God" (John 1:13; 1 John 3:9; 5:1), "is of God" (1 John 4:7) — spiritual origin, never biological paternity. When Paul means flesh he marks it: "made of the seed of David **according to the flesh**" (Romans 1:3, kata sarka, "according to the flesh"). Matthew 1:20 carries **no kata sarka** — the flesh-qualifier is absent.

[L2] The two verbs of Luke 1:35 are empowerment and presence words at every occurrence: eperchomai (G1904, "come upon") is the Pentecost word — "after that the Holy Ghost is **come upon** you, and ye shall be witnesses" (Acts 1:8; the power of Luke 24:49); episkiazō (G1982, "overshadow") is the transfiguration cloud (Luke 9:34 "a cloud overshadowed them") and Peter's healing shadow (Acts 5:15). [L3] 1 Samuel 16:13 "the Spirit of the LORD came upon David" — anointing.

These are covenant-origin and anointing words. The record does not make the Spirit a begetter of flesh. [L4, on the L2 verb-catalogue and the absent kata sarka marker above: the words the angel used are the words of anointing and divine presence, and the biological marker is missing where a paternity claim would require it.]

---

**IV. THE QUIET ROWS SAY LESS THAN WHAT IS CLAIMED ON THEM — [L1] + [L2] + [L3]**

[L1] "of whom was born Jesus" (Matthew 1:16) — [L2] egennēthē (G1080, "was born"), the one passive after thirty-nine active egennēsen ("begat") in the same genealogy: non-narration, not a denial of a man.

[L1] "How shall this be, seeing **I know not a man**?" (Luke 1:34) — [L2] andra ou ginōskō (G1097, "know"), present active indicative: a present state at the moment of speaking; she is betrothed (Luke 1:27), and [L3] twelve years later she says "thy father and I have sought thee" (Luke 2:48).

[L1] "before they came together" (Matthew 1:18); "knew her not **till** she had brought forth her firstborn son" (Matthew 1:25) — and Joseph names him (1:21, 1:25). Not one of these rows says "no man." Each is a present-state or sequencing statement, held as written — and none of them touches the father named in section II. [L4, on the L2 morphology and the L3 coexistence above: a present-tense statement and a "till" clause cannot be made to deny the father that the mother herself names.]

---

**V. "SON OF GOD" IS A COVENANT AND RESURRECTION TITLE — [L1] + [L3]**

[L1] "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Samuel 7:14) — spoken of Solomon, who had a living father. [L3] "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him to be my son" (1 Chronicles 28:6) — one verse, the son David begat and the title God gave him. [L1] "this day have I begotten thee" (Acts 13:33) — applied to the resurrection; "declared to be the Son of God... **by the resurrection**" (Romans 1:4). The title answers a covenant question; it never answers the biological one. [L4, on those footings: since the title is borne by a man with a living father and is attached to the resurrection, it cannot be read as a paternity statement.]

---

**VI. WHAT THE RECORD FORBIDS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — [L1]**

The text forbids "no man was involved" — the seed rows of section I forbid it. The text equally forbids narrating the how: no verse states the mechanics of the conception, and Matthew 1:18, 1:25 and Luke 1:34 stand exactly as written, beside the father the mother names (Luke 2:48) and the child Joseph names (Matthew 1:21, 25). The conclusion is the WHO, and the WHO is named.

---

**DECLARED CHAIN**

D1. The promised seed is David's own flesh-seed out of his body: [L1] Romans 1:3 "made of the seed of David according to the flesh"; 2 Samuel 7:12 "proceed out of thy bowels"; Acts 2:30 "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh"; [L2] sperma (G4690, "seed") with kata sarka ("according to the flesh"), osphys (G3751, "loins") as in Hebrews 7:5, 10; [L3] Psalm 132:11 "the fruit of thy body"; Hebrews 7:14 "our Lord sprang out of Juda."

D2. The father is named as a man in four registers: [L1] Luke 2:48 "thy father and I"; John 6:42 "the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know"; Matthew 1:20 "Joseph, thou son of David"; [L3] Luke 2:33 "Joseph and his mother"; Luke 4:22 "Is not this Joseph's son?"; John 1:45 "the son of Joseph."

D3. The Spirit-rows mark covenant origin and empowering presence, not begetting: [L2] ek (G1537, "of") with God/Spirit is spiritual-covenant origin (John 1:13; 1 John 4:7) and Matthew 1:20 lacks the kata sarka ("according to the flesh") marker Romans 1:3 carries; eperchomai (G1904, "come upon") is the Acts 1:8 anointing; episkiazō (G1982, "overshadow") is the Luke 9:34 cloud and the Acts 5:15 shadow; [L1] Matthew 1:20; Luke 1:35.

D4. The quiet rows are non-narration and present state, not a denial of a man: [L1] Matthew 1:16 "of whom was born Jesus," Luke 1:34 "I know not a man," Matthew 1:18 "before they came together," Matthew 1:25 "knew her not till," with Joseph naming the child (1:21, 25); [L2] egennēthē (G1080, "was born") one passive after thirty-nine active "begat"; andra ou ginōskō ("know not a man") present active indicative; [L3] Luke 2:48 "thy father" twelve years later.

D5. "Son of God" is a covenant and resurrection title, not a paternity claim: [L1] 2 Samuel 7:14 "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" of Solomon; Acts 13:33 "this day have I begotten thee" at the resurrection; Romans 1:4 "declared to be the Son of God... by the resurrection"; [L3] 1 Chronicles 28:6 "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him to be my son."

D6. ANSWER: Christ had a biological father — Joseph, the named Davidic father; a man was involved and the seed is honored through the named line, and the text does not narrate the how: [L1] Matthew 1:25 "thou shalt call his name JESUS" (Joseph's act); John 6:42 "the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know"; [L3] Romans 1:3 "the seed of David according to the flesh"; 2 Samuel 7:12 "out of thy bowels."

# CHALLENGE: Christ had no biological father. Joseph was his legal father, and the conception was of the Holy Ghost.

The standard reading holds that the child was conceived in Mary while she was a virgin, by the Holy Ghost, with no human father's seed. I take each of the defender's six sections in turn.

---

## 1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the genealogy's pattern, and the defender concedes it

[L1] "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, **of whom** was born Jesus, who is called Christ" (Matthew 1:16).

[L2] The relative pronoun hēs (G3739, "of whom") is **feminine singular**. It can only refer to Mary. The text does not say "Joseph begat Jesus." Joseph is called andra (G435, "husband"), not father. The defender admits that egennēthē (G1080, "was born") is "the one passive after thirty-nine active egennēsen ('begat')." He calls this "non-narration." But a writer who has said "begat" thirty-nine times and then changes verb, voice and pronoun gender at the one point where the chain would naturally continue has marked a break.

[L1] Luke supplies the explicit marker: "Jesus... being (**as was supposed**) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli" (Luke 3:23). [L2] enomizeto (G3543, "was thought, was reckoned by custom") is the verb of opinion. The narrator himself classifies the sonship as supposition.

[L4, on Matthew 1:16 (feminine hēs, passive after thirty-nine actives) and Luke 3:23 (enomizeto, "was supposed")]: two inspired genealogies decline to say Joseph begat him. One of them calls the Joseph-sonship a supposition. That is a positive limit on Joseph's fatherhood, not mere silence.

## 2. Jeremiah 22:30 bars a biological Joseph-line from the throne

[L1] Matthew traces Joseph through "Jechonias" (Matthew 1:11-12, 16). [L1] Of Coniah the LORD said: "Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for **no man of his seed** shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah" (Jeremiah 22:30). [L2] zera (H2233, "seed") is the same word as in 2 Samuel 7:12.

[L4, on Matthew 1:12, 16 (Joseph descends from Jechonias) and Jeremiah 22:30 (no seed of Coniah sits on David's throne)]: if the child were Joseph's biological seed, he would fall under that bar, yet Luke 1:32-33 promises him "the throne of his father David." The defender's reading collides with Jeremiah. The standard reading does not. Joseph supplies legal standing, and the seed comes by another route.

## 3. Matthew 1:18-25 locates the conception before Joseph and without him

[L1] "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, **before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost**" (1:18). [L1] "Joseph... was minded to put her away privily" (1:19). [L1] "**for** that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (1:20). [L1] "And knew her not **till** she had brought forth her firstborn son" (1:25).

- [L2] The verb in 1:20 is gennēthen (G1080, "that which is begotten, conceived"). It is the same verb as the "begat" of the genealogy, and here the agent is ek pneumatos hagiou ("out of the Holy Ghost"), the object is "in her" (en autē), and the thing is a conceived child, not an anointing.
- [L1] Joseph's problem in 1:19 is that she was found with child. If the child were his, there would be no dilemma. [L4, on 1:19 and the explanatory gar ("for") of 1:20]: the angel's "for" supplies the reason Joseph may take her. That reason works only if the pregnancy was not from a man.
- [L2] heōs hou (G2193 + G3739, "until which") in 1:25 bounds the entire period of conception and gestation: Joseph "knew her not." [L3] ginōskō (G1097, "know") carries the marital sense, as yada (H3045, "know") does in "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1). The text puts the conception **inside** the stretch where Joseph did not know her. What he does afterward is irrelevant to the question.

[L4, on the 1:18 chronology ("before they came together... found with child"), the 1:25 bound ("knew her not till"), and the gennēthen/ek pneumatos language]: the conception falls between two verses that both exclude Joseph's union with her, and the text assigns it to the Holy Ghost. The defender's section IV calls these "sequencing statements." But the sequence is the point. It puts the conception on the pre-union side of the line.

## 4. Luke 1:34-35 answers the how, and ties the title to it

[L1] "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (Luke 1:34). The angel does not say "Joseph shall come to thee." [L1] He says: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: **therefore also** that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God" (1:35).

- [L2] dio kai (G1352 + G2532, "wherefore also") makes the manner of conception the **cause** of the title. The defender's section V says the title "never answers the biological one." Luke 1:35 attaches the title to the conception.
- [L2] She is betrothed (1:27), so a question about "how" would be idle if Joseph were the expected means. The question presumes the conception is to be without a man, and the angel confirms it. The defender calls this a "present state." But the angel's reply is about a **future** conception with no future man mentioned.
- [L2] The defender catalogues episkiazō (G1982, "overshadow") as presence-and-power. I accept that. But the effect stated in the verse is "that holy thing which shall be born of thee." [L3] Hebrews 10:5 says: "a body hast thou **prepared** me" (katērtisō, G2675, "thou hast fitted, prepared"). The body is God's preparation.
- [L1] Acts 1:8 and 1 Samuel 16:13 describe the Spirit coming on persons already born. Luke 1:35 describes the Spirit coming on a woman before a child exists. The verb is the same, but the stated result differs, and the text states the result.

## 5. The seed rows do not require Joseph

[L1] Romans 1:3 reads "of the seed of David according to the flesh," and verse 4 follows with "according to the spirit of holiness." [L4, on Romans 1:3-4]: Paul sets two spheres side by side, flesh-descent from David and Spirit-sonship. He is not describing a single paternity.

- [L2] ek spermatos (G1537 + G4690, "out of the seed") names descent. It does not name Joseph. The defender's own parallels show this. [L1] Levi was "in the loins of Abraham" (Hebrews 7:10) across several generations. [L1] David is called Jesus' "father" (Luke 1:32) across about a thousand years. So "loins" and "father" language measures ancestry and does not require the nearest link to be a man.
- [L1] Acts 2:30 and Hebrews 7:14 name David and Judah, not Joseph.
- [L1] "God sent forth his Son, **made of a woman**" (Galatians 4:4). [L2] genomenon ek gynaikos (G1096 + G1537 + G1135, "come to be out of a woman") names only the woman as the human source. [L1] Elisabeth says "blessed is the fruit of thy womb" (Luke 1:42). [L3] "the seed of the woman" (Genesis 3:15, zera, H2233, "seed") is the one place the seed is reckoned through the woman, and Isaiah 7:14 echoes it: "the LORD himself shall give you **a sign**; Behold, a virgin shall conceive." A conception by an ordinary husband would be no sign. [L2] Matthew 1:23 renders the Hebrew almah (H5959, "young woman") by parthenos (G3933, "virgin"). Luke 1:27 uses the same word of Mary.

[L4, on Galatians 4:4 (woman only), Genesis 3:15 (the woman's seed), Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23 (sign; virgin)]: the Davidic flesh-line can come through Mary. Section I proves David's seed, not Joseph's.

## 6. The "four registers" are suppositions that the text itself corrects

- [L1] Luke 2:48, "thy father and I have sought thee." [L1] Jesus answers in the next verse: "wist ye not that I must be about **my Father's** business?" (2:49). The word "father" is answered by a different Father in the very next sentence.
- [L1] Matthew 13:55 and John 6:42 are the speeches of the unbelieving. In John 6:41-42 they "murmured." In Matthew 13:57 "they were offended in him." Luke 4:22 reports what the people said. [L1] "Whose father and mother we know" is the crowd's claim, not the narrator's verdict. [L3] John 1:45 is Philip's early, ordinary reckoning, offered before he understood who this was.
- [L1] Luke 2:33, "Joseph and his mother," and 2:41, "his parents," are the narrator's household usage. Luke 3:23, "as was supposed," sets the limit on that usage.
- [L1] Matthew 1:20, "Joseph, thou son of David," names Joseph's lineage, not the child's begetting. [L3] Naming without begetting is legal fatherhood. "She called his name Moses" (Exodus 2:10) was said of a child who "became her son." The levirate child "shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead" (Deuteronomy 25:6). [L1] Mordecai "took [Esther] for his own daughter" (Esther 2:7).

[L4, on Luke 2:48-49 (father/Father), Luke 3:23 (supposed), Exodus 2:10 and Deuteronomy 25:6 (legal naming and adoption)]: Joseph is father in the legal and household sense. The text sets that sense beside a limit ("supposed"), and it has the child himself answer "my Father."

## 7. Section V of the defender: the title cannot be flattened

[L1] Solomon's "I will be his father" (2 Samuel 7:14) was spoken of a son with a living human father. But Luke 1:35 says "**therefore** also... the Son of God" and ties the title to the conception. [L1] For Acts 13:33 the defender asserts "resurrection." But verse 34 adds, "that he raised him up **from the dead**," which verse 33 lacks. [L2] anastēsas (G450, "having raised up") in 13:33 is not the verb phrase of verse 34. [L4, on Luke 1:35 (dio kai) and Acts 13:33-34 (v.34 adds "from the dead")]: the defender's section V rests on one verse he reads as resurrection, while Luke 1:35 answers the origin question directly.

## 8. The defender's own parallel

[L1] The defender cites John 1:13: "born, **not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man**, but of God." [L2] There ek (G1537, "out of") with God is set in **antithesis** to ek thelēmatos andros ("out of the will of a man"). By the defender's own analogy, "of the Holy Ghost" in Matthew 1:20 excludes the man as source. It does not sit beside him.

---

## What I concede

[L1] Joseph is called "husband" (Matthew 1:16), "father" in the household sense (Luke 2:48), "son of David" (Matthew 1:20), and he names the child (1:25). All of that stands as **legal and household fatherhood**.

## Challenge chain

- **C1.** Matthew 1:16: hēs is feminine ("of whom"), Joseph is "husband" not begetter. Luke 3:23: "as was supposed" (enomizeto). The genealogies decline to say Joseph begat him.
- **C2.** Jeremiah 22:30 with Matthew 1:12: no seed of Coniah on David's throne, so Joseph's seed is excluded from the promise of Luke 1:32.
- **C3.** Matthew 1:18-20, 25: she "was found with child of the Holy Ghost" before they came together. "That which is conceived (gennēthen) in her is of (ek) the Holy Ghost." Joseph "knew her not till" the birth.
- **C4.** Luke 1:34-35: the answer to "how shall this be" is the Holy Ghost, and the title follows "therefore also." The body was "prepared" (Hebrews 10:5).
- **C5.** Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30 and Hebrews 7:14 name David and Judah, not Joseph. Galatians 4:4 and Luke 1:42 name the woman alone. Isaiah 7:14 calls it a sign.
- **C6.** The "father" speeches are the household's usage (Luke 2:48, answered by 2:49) or the crowd's claim (John 6:42; Matthew 13:55-57; Luke 4:22). Legal naming is not begetting (Exodus 2:10; Deuteronomy 25:6).
- **C7.** John 1:13 sets "of God" against "of the will of man."

**Questions the defender must answer from the text:**
1. Which verse says "Joseph begat Jesus"? Matthew 1:16 says it of Jacob and Joseph and then stops.
2. How can a biological Joseph-seed avoid Jeremiah 22:30?
3. Why does the angel's "for" in Matthew 1:20 comfort Joseph if the child were his?
4. What does "therefore also" in Luke 1:35 attach the title to, if not the conception?

**REPLY — DEFENDER, ROUND 2**

The challenger's case reads silence, sequence and titles as a denial of the named father. Each is answered by the verses around it. The claim I defend is the WHO: Christ had a biological father, Joseph, the named Davidic father. I narrate no how; neither does the text.

---

**I. C1 — MATTHEW 1:16 AND LUKE 3:23: NON-NARRATION AND CUSTOMARY RECKONING [L1] [L2] [L3]**

[L1] Matthew 1:16 falls at the seam of two forms of writing: the genealogy's "begat" chain ends, and the narrative opens at 1:18 — "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise." The birth is not narrated in the register's list form because Matthew narrates it in the paragraph after. [L2] egennēthē (G1080, "was born") is the same family verb as the thirty-nine active "begat"; a passive states a birth without naming the begetter — it does not negate one.

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli." [L2] enomizeto (G3543) is the lexicon's "to do by law (usage), i.e. to accustom; be wont" — the same verb form as Acts 16:13 "where prayer **was wont** to be made." The word reports customary reckoning and carries no verdict of its own; each context decides. [L3] In this same Gospel the narrator writes "his parents went to Jerusalem" (Luke 2:41) and Mary says "thy **father** and I have sought thee sorrowing" (2:48) — after twelve years. If "supposed" voided the fatherhood, the same author would not have the mother name him father afterwards. [L4, on the L2 gloss and the L3 rows in the same book: "as was supposed" marks the public reckoning; it does not erase the father the mother names.]

---

**II. C2 — JEREMIAH 22:30: THE BAR'S OWN BOUNDS, ITS REVERSAL, AND ITS REFLEXIVE EDGE [L1] [L3]**

[L1] "Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper **in his days**: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more **in Judah**" (Jeremiah 22:30). Two bounds are in the sentence: "in his days" and "in Judah." [L1] And the signet the sentence plucked off (22:24) is set back on: "In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, will I take thee, O Zerubbabel... and will make thee as a signet: **for I have chosen thee**" (Haggai 2:23) — Zerubbabel, "the son of Shealtiel," governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2). [L3] Jeremiah's own rule on pronounced sentences: "If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil" (Jeremiah 18:7-8). The New Testament names Jechonias twice (Matthew 1:11-12) and never cites this bar against Christ.

[L4, on the quoted bounds, the signet row and the Jeremiah 18 rule: the sentence is bounded, answered in its own book, and uncited by the apostles.]

And the bar cuts the challenger's case at least as hard as mine: he grants Joseph "legal standing" as "son of David" (Matthew 1:20) — that standing is the descent the genealogy gives through Jechonias (Matthew 1:12, 16). A bar on "his seed" sitting on David's throne does not open a door for the same line to hand the throne over by law. Yet the throne is not seized by line at all: "the Lord God shall **give** unto him the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32) — given by God, while the seed is flesh (Romans 1:3). The challenger's question 2 assumes inheritance by succession; the text says give.

---

**III. C3 — MATTHEW 1:18-25: WHAT THE ROWS ACTUALLY STATE [L1] [L2]**

[L1] "before they came together, she was found with child" (1:18) — a state at the espousal, stated as it stood. [L1] "Joseph... being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily" (1:19) — [L2] dikaios ōn, mē thelōn, eboulēthē: a character, a refusal, an intent. No verb of knowing is in the row; the text records what Joseph willed, not what he knew, and Matthew names no statute to explain him. Question 3 asks why the angel's "for" comforts him if the child were his: the "for" is "that which is conceived in her is **of (ek) the Holy Ghost**" (1:20) — and [L2] ek (G1537) with God or Spirit is the covenant-origin idiom at every New Testament row ("born of God," John 1:13; 1 John 3:9; "is of God," 1 John 4:7) — the child is of God's covenant purpose, and the angel's commission to Joseph is a father's act: "**thou shalt call his name JESUS**" (1:21), done at 1:25. [L3] The same father-naming is commanded at Luke 1:13 and performed at 1:62-63 ("they made signs to his father, how he would have him called").

[L1] "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (1:25) is held exactly as written: it bounds the time to the birth and says nothing after. [L2] ginōskō (G1097, "know") carries the marital sense at Genesis 4:1 — granted. But the row states Joseph's conduct; it does not narrate the conception, and no row in the passage says "no man."
